episode.lensDescription: Practical strategies educators can use now
episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Wednesday, April 15, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, new Gallup data reveals a significant shift in how young adults view artificial intelligence. Gen Z's excitement about A.I. dropped 14 points over the past year to just 22 percent. Hopefulness fell nine points to 18 percent, while anger rose nine points to 31 percent. Perhaps most telling: the decline is sharpest among daily A.I. users, who saw excitement fall 18 points compared to last year.

The disconnect between schools and workplaces may explain some of this anxiety. More than half of college students surveyed say their school either discourages A.I. use or outright bans it. Meanwhile, 63 percent of faculty surveyed by the American Association of Colleges and Universities believe their 2025 graduates were not prepared to use A.I. at work. Sixteen percent of currently enrolled college students have changed their major due to A.I., according to Gallup.

The job market adds pressure. Federal Reserve data shows the unemployment rate for recent college graduates reached 5.7 percent in the fourth quarter of 2025, above the national rate. Underemployment hit 42.5 percent, the highest since 2020. A Harvard working paper tracking 62 million workers found that at companies adopting A.I., junior hiring fell nearly 8 percent within six quarters, not through layoffs, but through a quiet freeze on new positions.

The Harvard researchers noted that the hiring decline was concentrated in entry-level positions, with experienced workers largely unaffected.

Some efforts are emerging to address the gap. Khan Academy, the TED conference, and testing company E.T.S. announced this week a ten-thousand-dollar interactive online program to train students for A.I.-era jobs. IBM announced earlier this year it is tripling entry-level hiring, predicting A.I. will expand what new workers do.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, an op-ed in University Business argues that A.I. writing tools may be democratizing access to professional communication. The piece recounts a fast-food worker whose social media post drew sharp criticism not for its ideas, but for how it was written. When advised to use A.I. to reword future posts, she welcomed the suggestion.

The author contends that communication skills function as social currency accumulated through formal education. Those fluent in academic norms benefit while others are quietly excluded. A.I. tools now give people access to communicative power that once required years of formal training.

The piece raises uncomfortable questions for higher education: Are institutions assessing critical thinking, or simply fluency in elite communication norms? If A.I. use is acceptable across the professional world, from drafting emails to writing reports to coding, why prohibit it for students preparing to enter that world? The author asks whether educators are concerned that A.I. devalues learning, or simply unsettled by the shift in who gets to be heard.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation, Grand Valley State University leaders are defending the school's one hundred sixty-six million dollar investment in technology and A.I.-related education as necessary to prepare students for the modern workforce, according to Crain's Grand Rapids. Four past and present university presidents gathered April 15 at the Loosemore Auditorium on GVSU's downtown Grand Rapids campus to discuss stewardship of the institution. The presidents included Philomena Mantella, Thomas Haas, Mark Murray, and Arend Don Lubbers. The investment represents one of the largest publicly disclosed commitments to A.I.-focused education infrastructure at a regional public university in Michigan.

<break time="1.0s"/>

From our Case Study file, San Diego State University's Imperial Valley campus is redesigning two mathematics courses using Adobe A.I. tools through a California State University systemwide initiative. The thirty-thousand-dollar grant, awarded to 22 C.S.U. campuses per cycle, supports a three-semester pilot integrating Adobe Express and A.I. tools into statistics and calculus courses.

In the statistics course, students complete projects using Excel for data analysis, then transform their computational work into visual projects using Adobe Express and Firefly. In calculus, students will create visual explanations of derivatives and rates of change using video and animation tools. The project team includes principal investigators Tingting Tang and Weichen Zhao, with course instructors Huan Qin and Christopher Ryan. The initiative aims to help students from nursing, criminal justice, and liberal studies who may struggle with required math courses, shifting the focus from equations alone to a more visual, storytelling approach.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Gallup Data Shows Gen Z Excitement About AI Dropped 14 Points in One Year
leadStory.summary:
According to Gallup polling released last week, Gen Z's excitement about artificial intelligence dropped 14 points over the past year to just 22 percent. Hopefulness about the technology fell nine points to 18 percent, while anger rose nine points to 31 percent.

The sentiment decline is sharper among those who use AI most frequently. Daily AI users in the cohort saw excitement fall 18 points and hopefulness tumble 11 points compared to last year.

More than half of college students surveyed in a separate Gallup poll say their school either discourages AI use (42 percent) or outright bans it (11 percent). Meanwhile, 63 percent of faculty surveyed by the American Association of Colleges and Universities believe their schools' 2025 graduates were not prepared to use AI at work.

The job market adds pressure. Federal Reserve data pegged the unemployment rate for recent college graduates at 5.7 percent in the fourth quarter of 2025, above the national rate. Underemployment for recent graduates reached 42.5 percent, the highest since 2020.

A Harvard working paper tracking 62 million workers found that at companies adopting AI, junior hiring fell nearly 8 percent within six quarters, not through layoffs but through a freeze on new positions.

Some efforts are emerging. Khan Academy, the TED conference, and testing company ETS announced a ten-thousand-dollar interactive online program to train students for AI-era jobs. IBM announced it is tripling entry-level hiring, predicting AI will expand what new workers do.

quickHits.headline: Op-Ed Argues AI Writing Tools Democratize Access to Professional Communication
quickHits.summary:
An op-ed in University Business argues that generative AI tools can interrupt a cycle where people are penalized for communication gaps unrelated to intelligence or capability.

The piece recounts a fast-food worker named Sara whose social media post drew criticism not for its ideas but for how it was written. When advised to use AI to reword future posts, she welcomed the suggestion with enthusiasm.

The author contends that communication skills function as social currency accumulated through formal education systems. Those fluent in academic norms reap benefits while others are excluded. AI tools, the argument goes, now give people access to communicative power that once required years of formal training.

The piece raises questions for higher education: Are institutions assessing critical thinking or simply fluency in elite communication norms? If AI use is acceptable across the professional world, why prohibit it for students preparing to enter that world?

Four past and present university presidents gathered April 15 at the Loosemore Auditorium on GVSU's downtown Grand Rapids Robert C. Pew campus to discuss stewardship of the institution. The presidents pictured include Philomena Mantella, Thomas Haas, Mark Murray, and Arend "Don" Lubbers.

quickHits.headline: SDSU Imperial Valley Faculty Redesign Math Courses Using Adobe AI Tools
quickHits.summary:
San Diego State University's Imperial Valley campus is redesigning two mathematics courses using Adobe AI tools through a California State University systemwide initiative, according to SDSU News.

The thirty-thousand-dollar grant, awarded to 22 CSU campuses per cycle, supports a three-semester pilot integrating Adobe Express and AI tools into mathematics and statistics courses. The pilot begins this spring with Statistical Principles and Practices, followed by Calculus I, and concludes with a refined iteration in fall 2026 and spring 2027.

In the statistics course, students complete a class project using Excel for data analysis, then pair their computational work with Adobe Express and Firefly to transform raw data into visual projects. In calculus, students will use Adobe Express Video and animation tools to create visual explanations of derivatives and rates of change.

The project team includes principal investigators Tingting Tang and Weichen Zhao, with course instructors Huan Qin and Christopher Ryan. The initiative aims to help students from nursing, criminal justice, and liberal studies who may struggle with required math courses.
